newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Rains ease Sri Lanka power crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rains ease Sri Lanka power crisis.

text.p: Recent rains have raised water levels in Sri Lanka's hydropower reservoirs to comfortable levels, a Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) state power utility official said on Tuesday.
"We have no problem at the moment. The hydropower supply level is very sound," he said. "We had an inflow of 16 GwH (gigawatt hours) on Monday."
Storage in hydropower reservoirs was around 477 GwH or 38 percent of the total hydroreservoir storage, he said.
The island has scaled down thermal power production after heavy rains began filling hydropower reservoirs, which supply up to 85 percent of electricity.
"There's no reason to believe we'll have a power supply problem this year," the CEB official said. "However, we still expect two more seasons of rain."
A Meteorology Department official said recent rains were caused by a cyclone in the Bay of Bengal, which was now dissipating.
"We're still waiting for the monsoon rains," deputy director P.M. Jayatilaka Banda told Reuters. "Our wind pattern might change once the cyclone dissipates."

Reservoir water levels fell to dangerously low levels with the failure of the November-March northeast monsoon for the second straight year, and weak intermonsoon showers, prompting the CEB to raise thermal power generation to meet the shortfall and avoid power cuts.
The island endured daily power cuts of up to eight hours at the height of the drought last year.
Sri Lanka has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for hydroelectric plants, usually begins in the third week of May.
The CEB has said it plans to cut dependence on hydropower to 57 percent of the total requirement by building more thermal power plants by June this year.
The island now has a permanent installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power, produced mainly by diesel plants.
